rq5.open_problems.sonnet: The paper asks whether practical ID schemes can be proven secure under Fiat-Shamir with a specific hash function. It also asks whether another secure general transformation exists, and whether Fiat-Shamir fails for ID schemes with unconditional soundness.

cq.note.opus: Weak Fiat-Shamir that does not hash the statement breaks adaptive soundness. Commitment generators are created with a known discrete log, which gives a trapdoor for faking the shuffle. The facts the ZKPs prove are not enough for vote validity. The MPC is not secure against collusion. Several other mixnet libraries are also reviewed for how they generate parameters.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The authors inspected only a small fraction of a very complex code base. They did not implement the fake decryption proof inside the full mixing sequence.
rq5.limitations.opus: The authors inspected only a small fraction of a complex codebase and did not thoroughly examine the remediations. Some attacks rely on ambiguous spec interpretation or leave invalid votes behind, and the fake decryption proof was not integrated into the full sequence.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The implementation omits zero-knowledge sumcheck, Orion and aggregation, and is not parallelized. Proof size is large compared with generic IVCs, memory use is hundreds of GB, and AlexNet and VGG-11 were truncated. Generic IVC baselines were extrapolated rather than run.
rq5.limitations.opus: The implementation does not include ZK variants of sumcheck, Orion or aggregation, and is not parallelized; the proof is larger than in generic IVCs and peak memory reaches hundreds of GB. rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: Proximity gaps (correlated agreement) for Reed-Solomon codes: if many z give f+z·g close to C, then [f,g] is close to C^2, with a reduced number a of exceptional z. This lowers soundness error for FRI/STARK-type proximity tests.

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: Proximity gaps are the soundness basis for FRI, STIR, WHIR, Basefold and STARK-based zkVMs; tighter bounds reduce field size and soundness error.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Proximity gaps determine soundness error of hash-based arguments used on blockchains

cq.note.sonnet: Gives counterexamples refuting n^τ-bounded proximity gaps (Conjecture 1.2) and a prover attack on the DEEP-ALI STARK for CYCLE-SUM (Theorem 1.20) showing the soundness bound cannot be improved much. These are soundness limits, not a standard failure class.
cq.note.opus: Gives a prover attack on STARK for CYCLE-SUM AIR showing soundness ≥ Ω(1/n) at list-decoding radius; refutes the n^τ-bounded proximity gaps conjecture.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: Positive results hold only up to the Johnson radius, and the negative results rely on specific code and field constructions (characteristic 2, special prime-field subgroups). Several results depend on Conjecture 1.14 or are proved only in the full version.
rq5.limitations.opus: Positive results only go up to the Johnson radius; prime-field negative results rely on unproven Conjecture 1.14.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Whether proximity gaps hold beyond the Johnson radius for prime fields or well-chosen evaluation domains, and whether the list-decoding radius of Reed-Solomon codes exceeds the Johnson radius.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Proximity gaps beyond the Johnson radius, which need better list-decoding bounds; whether the conjecture holds over prime fields or for well-chosen domains in characteristic 2.

rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Non-malleable proofs with black-box extraction are needed to link evaluated ciphertexts to their inputs and to reduce security to CCA2; succinctness preserves compactness

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The transformation is fully generic and not instantiated or evaluated, so concrete efficiency is unknown. Approximate FHE needs CPAD-secure starting schemes. rq5.limitations.opus: vCCA conflicts with circuit privacy, and designated-verifier variants achieve only relaxed compactness. Approximate FHE requires CPAD security, and the transformation is generic with no concrete instantiation.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Find FHE schemes, embeddings and SNARKs (e.g., ring-native SNARKs) that fit together efficiently, and explore circuit privacy definitions for security beyond CCA1. Is there a stronger meaningful notion than vCCA that FHE can achieve?
rq5.open_problems.opus: Open problems are jointly choosing compatible FHE schemes, embeddings and SNARKs (e.g., ring-native SNARKs), and achieving circuit privacy beyond CCA1. It is also open whether a notion stronger than vCCA is achievable for FHE.

rq5.open_problems.opus: More aggressive d-split parameters, more cryptanalysis of SD over extension and non-binary fields, and prime-field instances using the NTT. Implementations using dedicated F256 instructions are also left open.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: Results require prime-order groups. Decisional assumptions are not captured, since distinguishers are trivially algebraic. rq5.limitations.opus: All results require prime-order groups, and decisional problems are captured only trivially because distinguishers output bits. Oblivious sampling of group elements is not covered, and it is open whether the AGM inherits ROM/GGM-style weaknesses.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Whether the AGM suffers from Dent-style pathologies, how to extend it to composite-order and pairing groups, and how to model decisional adversaries. Further open items are classifying assumptions within the AGM and automating AGM proofs.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Extending the AGM to composite-order groups, classifying further assumptions, and building automated AGM proof tools. Another open question is whether iO-based non-extractable algebraic one-way functions invalidate the AGM.

rq3.speedup_and_baseline.sonnet: No speedup reported. Size comparison: a prototype using MAC_GGM with exponential Elgamal gave 600+ byte ciphertexts for a 16-byte UID, versus 64 bytes here. The text also gives 288-byte ciphertexts for an eight-element variant.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline.opus: 64-byte ciphertext vs 600+ bytes (288-byte ciphertext elsewhere) in an earlier MAC_GGM + exponential Elgamal prototype; pairing about 40x and RSA-3072 about 50x the cost of a Ristretto scalar multiplication

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: The user holds a valid server-issued credential (auth or profile key) whose certified UID/profile key attributes match the submitted Elgamal-like ciphertexts under the group key, without revealing the UID.
rq4.statement_proven.opus: Possession of a valid KVAC credential whose attributes (UID, profile key) are the plaintexts of given deterministic ciphertexts under the group public params

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: Non-interactive generalized Schnorr proofs of knowledge (Fiat-Shamir) over ristretto255, with a new algebraic-MAC KVAC and symmetric deterministic verifiable encryption.
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Generic linear Schnorr proofs made non-interactive with Fiat-Shamir

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: Prime-order group only, with no pairings or strong RSA. Group-element attributes enable efficient verifiable encryption, giving small ciphertexts and fast proofs.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Everything stays in one prime-order group with no pairings or strong RSA, so it is efficient and uses the same curve Signal already uses

cq.note.sonnet: Scheme design addresses consistency and unique-ciphertext requirements. It does not study ZK failure classes such as bugs or attacks.
cq.note.opus: No study of ZK failure classes.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The server can observe which encrypted entries perform actions, and can delete or reinstate old ciphertexts. A removed member who holds the GroupMasterKey can collude with the server. The MAC proof relies on the generic group model for MAC_GGM, and the system-level proof is only a sketch.
rq5.limitations.opus: The server can see access patterns and can delete or roll back ciphertexts, and removed users who keep the master key can collude with the server. MAC security relies on the generic group model, and the system security proof is only a sketch.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Prove the MAC secure under DDH alone, make the system-level simulation proof rigorous, and remove the generic group model assumption. Also add end-to-end integrity, automated rekeying, and formal-methods analysis.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Replace the GGM assumption with DDH, make the system-level proof rigorous, and apply formal or automated analysis. Add end-to-end integrity and re-keying.

rq4.statement_proven.opus: Knowledge of square roots mod n of identity values (passport identification)

cq.note.sonnet: Covers mafia fraud, renting passports, multiple identities and subliminal channels. Prevention is an active-warden protocol. Detection of the channels is argued to be infeasible.
cq.note.opus: Identifies the mafia (relay) fraud, multiple identities, passport renting and undetectable subliminal channels. Proposes an active-warden protocol to make the protocol subliminal-free.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: Security proofs are deferred to other papers [6], and the active-warden solution needs a trusted warden and assumes no extra unwatched channels. The mafia fraud and passport renting are not solved by the paper's own scheme.
rq5.limitations.opus: Proofs are deferred to [6]. The active-warden solution needs a trusted warden and assumes there are no unwatched extra channels.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Better passport protocols that do only identification (cited works [5], [14]) are expected. Subliminal channels in other ZK protocols are left to the reader and to [6].
rq5.open_problems.opus: Subliminal channels inside j or the identity are not addressed. Better passport protocols, including identification over the telephone, are expected.

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: The prover holds a model consistent with commitment c_M that was trained by the specified logistic regression algorithm on a dataset consistent with commitment c_D.
rq4.statement_proven.opus: The committed model was trained with SGD logistic regression on the committed dataset using the committed randomness

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: MPC-in-the-head over a packed-secret-sharing MPC, combined with FRI-based list polynomial commitments and univariate sumcheck and permutation checks.
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Custom MPC-in-the-head over packed secret sharing plus FRI-based polynomial commitment, univariate sumcheck and PLONK permutation check (winterfell)

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: MPCitH handles non-arithmetic operations (truncation, comparison) and has fast proving. SNARK techniques shrink the proof to be sublinear in the data and avoid the memory and prover overhead of generic zkSNARKs.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Balances prover time against proof size; hash-based, avoids elliptic-curve operations; streaming-friendly memory use

rq5.limitations.opus: The scheme uses a modified training algorithm (piecewise-linear activation, fixed-point arithmetic), and its proofs are much larger than SNARK proofs. Offline-phase times were not benchmarked and the preprocessing is expensive.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Extending zkPoT to more complex models such as CNNs, avoiding the large field (for example a 64-bit field), and reducing cryptographic overhead and proof size.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Extending zkPoT to CNNs and other larger models, and using a 64-bit field and a streaming implementation to cut costs.

rq2.proof_size.sonnet: Communication per client O(nL + n log(L) + n^2); proof part O(n log(L) + n) after batching
rq2.proof_size.opus: O(n log(L) + n) proof communication per client after batching

rq2.verifier_cost.opus: O(nL) per client; server O(nL + n)

rq3.workload.sonnet: Aggregation integrity checks (Multi-Krum, SignGuard, rank-based and similarity-based) on Fashion-MNIST (LeNet-5, 60K parameters) and CIFAR-10 (ResNet-20, 273K parameters). Tested with up to 200 clients (400 for key distribution) and 500-10,000 proof parameters.
rq3.workload.opus: Verifiable FL aggregation (degree-two relations over secret shares) with 1,000-10,000 parameters, up to 200-400 clients; LeNet-5 on Fashion-MNIST, ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10

rq3.speedup_and_baseline.sonnet: No speedup over a ZK baseline is reported. Online ZKP checking takes <3 s for 200 clients with 1,000 parameters. Accuracy is 85% on Fashion-MNIST and 70-85% on CIFAR-10, versus 5% and 3% with no defense.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline.opus: Under 3 s for 200 clients with 1,000 parameters; accuracy 70-85% vs 3-5% for FL with no defense; no runtime baseline

rq3.memory.sonnet: 44 MB per client and 61 MB for the server (200 clients, 1,000 parameters). Distance calculation peaks at 2.3 GB of total message volume.
rq3.memory.opus: 44 MB per client and 61 MB for the server (200 clients, 1,000 parameters); up to 2.3 GB total data shares for distance calculations

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: Each client's shared multiplication triples satisfy c = sum of a_k*b_k (degree-two relation), so that the input models and the aggregation computations (norm bound, ranking, distance) are correct.
rq4.statement_proven.opus: Correctness of aggregation predicate computations (degree-two relations/multiplication triples) over secret-shared client model updates

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: Secret-sharing-based distributed ZKP (G-gate polynomial consistency checks with Shamir/VSS, Fiat-Shamir for the online phase) over a Chord P2P overlay
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Distributed ZK proofs on secret shares (G-gate polynomial checks, Fiat-Shamir) with verifiable Shamir secret sharing

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: Supports aggregation rules that need client interaction, with sublinear proof communication, no single point of failure, and a one-third Byzantine tolerance.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Supports multiple verifiers over shared data with sublinear proof communication and tolerates up to (n-1)/3 malicious clients

cq.note.sonnet: The paper defends against Byzantine and poisoning clients, not ZKP implementation failures.
cq.note.opus: NR

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The scheme applies only to horizontal or P2P FL, not vertical FL without PKI. The offline phase grows quadratically with the number of clients, Multi-Krum is costly (260-550 s per iteration) and is weak against ALIE, and SignGuard sign features are processed in plaintext.
rq5.limitations.opus: Does not apply to vertical FL without a PKI; offline preprocessing grows quadratically with the number of clients, and Multi-Krum is slow and less effective against ALIE.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Secure vertical FL, in particular fairness of secret-shared labels and the cost of tree-based VFL. Also incentive mechanisms and a server-less P2P variant.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Extending to P2P FL without a server, secure VFL with fair secret-shared labels, and incentive mechanisms.

rq2.proof_size.opus: 288-byte proof + ~71-byte ECDSA signature = 359 bytes

rq3.workload.opus: Medical insurance premium circuits: linear regression, logistic regression, SVM, and 3-layer NN, with 10-50 private inputs (4-20 for the NN)

rq3.speedup_and_baseline.opus: No speedup reported; analytical comparison with ADSNARK (k vs nk signatures and verifications). Fixing NN parameters cut execution time to ~1/7 and gas to ~1/20 of the unfixed NN.

rq3.memory.opus: Proving keys 10 MB to 90 MB; verification keys at most tens of KB

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: The output y is computed from private data x via circuit C, and hash h of (x, metadata a) is computed from the same x. h carries a data authenticator's signature, so the data is authentic.
rq4.statement_proven.opus: Output y is computed by circuit C from private data x, and h = H(x, a) is a hash of x and its metadata a, where h is signed by a trusted data authenticator

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: zk-DASNARK, built on a simulation-extractable zk-SNARK (GM17) plus a digital signature. Implemented with libsnark and xJsnark on alt_bn128.
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: zk-SNARK (GM17-style simulation-extractable; libsnark on alt_bn128 with xJsnark) plus ECDSA signature

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: One hash circuit and one signature replace per-input signature verification (as in ADSNARK). Proofs are short and cheap for on-chain verification.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Succinct proofs and fast verification suit on-chain checking. Signing a single hash outside the circuit avoids verifying signatures inside the circuit and avoids ADSNARK's per-input signatures.

cq.note.sonnet: NR
cq.note.opus: NR

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The scheme needs a trusted data authenticator and a trusted CRS generator. The output y and the payment amount are public, and the SHA256 circuit enlarges the proving key and increases prover cost.
rq5.limitations.opus: The scheme relies on a trusted data authenticator and leaks the computation output y (payment amount). The SHA256 circuit makes proving keys large, the Ethereum block gas limit had to be removed, and public inputs are capped at about 1,200.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Hiding the output and payment, for example by combining with Zerocash, and supporting multiple data authenticators. Authority-free data authentication remains only partially addressed.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Hiding the payment output by combining with Zerocash-style circuits, supporting multiple authenticators, using cheaper hashes such as MiMC, and authority-free authentication.

rq2.prover_cost.opus: Quasi-linear T·polylog(T); SHA-256 block 73.86 s

rq3.workload.opus: TERMinator benchmarks (SPECK, SIMON, Factorial, Fibonacci, Collatz, matrix multiplication, PIR), SHA-256, Vickrey auction, range proof

rq4.statement_proven.opus: Correct execution of a zMIPS program on public and private tapes yields output y within T steps

rq4.proof_system_used.opus: zk-STARK (libSTARK)

rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Transparent setup, plausible post-quantum security, and reliance only on CRHF and ROM

rq5.limitations.opus: Prover and verifier costs are about an order of magnitude higher than Bulletproofs/Hyrax, because computations are compiled from ZeroJava to zMIPS rather than written as arithmetic circuits. Memory accesses add permutation constraints that dominate cost as T grows.

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: The server knows (K, a, s, ru, rv, a_l^-1) consistent with the input-independent Legendre symbols and with the hash values cu, cv of the VOLE+ inputs u, v, so it behaved honestly in the Legendre function evaluation.

rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Quicksilver (VOLE-based ZK) together with VOLE+ built from subset VOLE and Kyber-based OT

rq5.limitations.opus: Security proofs are in the classical ROM, and the timing omits network latency. Verifiability is only conjectured, not proven.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Prove security in the QROM, formally add verifiability and threshold versions to the framework, and tighten the DSLS reduction so a smaller prime can be used. Reduce communication via batched base OTs or power residue symbols, and weaken the F_SFE functionality.
rq5.open_problems.opus: A security analysis in the QROM, a tighter DSLS reduction, and verifiable or threshold extensions. Also power residue symbols and batched base OTs.

rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Homomorphic verifiable tags (BLS-like) combined with a KZG polynomial commitment: the PLONK batch variant in the basic scheme and PCS-MPAP in the batch scheme, verified by a smart contract

rq5.open_problems.opus: Further reducing the computation overhead of on-chain verification.

rq3.workload.sonnet: Compiling 77 Circom-library circuits re-implemented in Coda to R1CS; comparison of constraint counts
rq3.workload.opus: 77 circuits from 9 Circom projects (circomlib, circom-bigint, Semaphore, Sismo, ZK-SBT, Darkforest-eth, ZK-SQL, Circomlib-ml, ed25519-circom)

rq3.speedup_and_baseline.sonnet: No speedup. Versus Circom -O1, Coda generates equal or fewer constraints for 100% of benchmarks. Versus Circom -O2, 82% of benchmarks are within 10% of Circom's constraint count and 26% have equal or fewer constraints.
rq3.speedup_and_baseline.opus: Compared with Circom -O1, Coda produces equal or fewer constraints on 100% of benchmarks. Compared with Circom -O2, it is within 10% on 82% of benchmarks and equal or fewer on 26%. Proofs are 60% shorter than with Coq shallow embedding. Average type-check time is about 177-184 ms.

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: Functional correctness of ZK arithmetic circuits (e.g. BigLessThan output equals 1 iff |a|<|b|), expressed as refinement types and discharged as Coq lemmas
rq4.statement_proven.opus: Functional correctness of Circom-style arithmetic circuits (e.g., BigLessThan, BigMod, ed25519 components) against refinement-type specifications

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: R1CS output for existing zkSNARK backends via zkInterface; no proof system of its own
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: R1CS output in zkInterface format for existing zkSNARK backends

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: R1CS is the target because existing zkSNARK generators can produce a prover and verifier from R1CS constraints
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Existing zkSNARK generators can produce a prover and verifier from R1CS constraints

cq.note.sonnet: Unprovable Coq obligations exposed 6 previously unknown bugs in Circom circuits (missing range check, zero considered positive, missing logical constraints), all confirmed by developers. The type system is proven sound.
cq.note.opus: Found 6 previously unknown bugs caused by missing constraints (e.g., a missing range check in BigMod, zero treated as positive in IsPositive). Developers confirmed all of them.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: Type checking is not decidable and the Coq lemmas need manual proofs for some obligations; loop invariants must be annotated by hand. 66 of 77 circuits were verified, the circuits were translated manually from Circom, and the compiler itself is not certified.
rq5.limitations.opus: SMT solvers cannot handle prime-field polynomial reasoning, so manual Coq proofs are sometimes needed. Loop invariants must be annotated by hand, and not all obligations were discharged (93% of correct circuits were verified).

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Integrating specialized solvers for polynomial equations over finite fields to increase proof automation. A certified compilation from Coda to R1CS is also left open.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Certifying the Coda compiler itself, and adding finite-field solvers to improve proof automation.

rq2.prover_cost.opus: NR

rq3.workload.opus: DKG-CL/DKG-DL and threshold ECDSA offline signing on secp256k1 with a CL-HSMq class group (256-bit plaintext space, 1827-bit ΔK, 128-bit security), n∈{5,10,15,20}

[48] (NDSS '23); Paillier-based [11] offline communication is 153 KB (n=5) and 613 KB (n=20), at least twice the CL-based schemes; OT-based Gagol et al. rq3.speedup_and_baseline.opus: Over half of the runtime and total communication saved vs Wong et al. [48]; about 20% less offline communication vs Castagnos et al. [16]; the Paillier-based scheme [11] needs 153 KBytes (n=5) and 613 KBytes (n=20) offline, at least twice the CLE-based schemes; the OT-based scheme [35] takes half the runtime but more communication (~400 KBytes at 15 parties, ~700 KBytes at 20)

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: Well-formedness of CL ciphertexts and commitments, correct (partial) decryption, discrete log in class groups, and multiplication of ciphertexts by a committed or encrypted secret, supporting robust threshold ECDSA and BBS+ signing and DKG.
rq4.statement_proven.opus: Well-formedness of CL encryptions and commitments, correct (partial) decryption, discrete logarithm in class groups, and correct homomorphic multiplication of ciphertexts

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: Fiat–Shamir NIZK and multi-party Σ-protocols with equivocable commitments over class groups, plus Pedersen commitments and dual-code share verification
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Σ-protocols (Fiat–Shamir NIZK with SHA-3) and a multi-party Σ-protocol in class groups and ECC groups

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: Public verifiability and non-interactive fault attribution; witness extraction in unknown-order class groups for dishonest-majority simulation; avoids range proofs because the CL message space is Z_q.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Public verifiability and witness extraction in an unknown-order group, needed for non-interactive fault attribution and for simulation under a dishonest majority

cq.note.sonnet: Not a bug-finding paper. It designs robust DKG and signing so faults are identified and removed without restart, and notes that complex ZKPs in prior MtA schemes are error-prone.
cq.note.opus: The paper only remarks that complex ZKPs (e.g., range proofs) are error-prone; it does not study such failures itself.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: Security is game-based and static-corruption, not UC. Class-group DKG is the costliest part, and the scheme needs stable broadcast channels.
rq5.limitations.opus: DKG for class groups is the most costly part of the scheme. The scheme relies on stable broadcast channels and does not achieve UC security.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Upgrading to UC security and simplifying the class-group DKG, possibly to a one-round DKG if a biased key is tolerated. Exploring weaker communication assumptions.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Achieving UC security and a one-round (possibly asynchronous) DKG for threshold CL encryption. Exploring weaker communication assumptions.

rq2.proof_size.opus: Total authentication messages (2368 + 320 × nBIDb) bits

rq3.memory.opus: Device storage (672 + 544 × n_s + 64 × |S_UIDu|) bits; on-chain binding certificate (1120 + 320 × nBIDb) bits; cuckoo filter about 32 KB per 10,000 elements

rq4.statement_proven.opus: Knowledge of the biometric key k_bio and the binding key k_bk opening the on-chain Pedersen commitment Commit = k_bio·P + k_bk·Q

rq4.proof_system_used.sonnet: Pedersen-commitment-based Sigma-style ZKPoK (Fiat-Shamir style challenge t = H2(E||N2)) plus a Schnorr signature, with CRT, PUF-based KDF/BIP-32, cuckoo filter and a Hyperledger Fabric blockchain
rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Pedersen-commitment-based ZKPoK (Schnorr-style, with the challenge t = H2(E||N2) using server nonce N2), plus Schnorr signatures with BIP-32 pseudo-keys

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: Lightweight authentication on devices that hides the biometric and binding keys while avoiding the pairing-heavy group/ring signatures
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: To authenticate the user and any bound device as a whole with conditional anonymity, without bilinear pairings on the device

cq.note.sonnet: The paper studies no ZKP failure class. The cuckoo filter blocks malicious logins from unregistered pseudo-keys, and the paper discusses a false-positive rate of about 3%.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: The communication cost grows linearly with the number of bound devices (heaviest at nBIDb ≥ 13, so binding groups should be limited to about 7). rq5.limitations.opus: Communication cost grows linearly with the number of bound devices, so the paper recommends at most about 7 per group. The trusted authority (TA) is a single point of failure, and the blockchain throughput (50 TPS) limits the non-authentication phases.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Design a specialized blockchain (new architecture, optimized consensus) for large-scale deployment. Design a distributed binding-key generation method using Shamir secret sharing to remove the TA single point of failure.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Designing a specialised blockchain for large-scale deployment. Distributed binding-key generation via Shamir secret sharing to remove the TA single point of failure.

rq4.proof_system_used.opus: Modified Camenisch-Lysyanskaya signature with a Fiat-Shamir NIZK, plus Cramer-Shoup encryption, in bilinear groups

rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Needs only one end-to-end wireless transmission, keeps vehicles anonymous and unlinkable against semi-trusted RSUs, and supports batch verification

rq3.workload.opus: Six ML algorithms (linear and logistic regression, NN, SVM, K-Means, decision tree) on BHP, US census, MNIST and Nursery datasets, batch sizes 32/64/128

rq4.statement_proven.sonnet: A sampled training iteration was correctly executed, mapping the previous state and a data batch to an output state that matches the committed hash identifier. This lets the client verify the training workload without learning the model.
rq4.statement_proven.opus: Sampled SGD/training iterations (or a prediction) were computed correctly from a committed blinded state, i.e., a hash of the random-weighted sum of the state

rq4.proof_system_used.opus: QAP-based SNARK via jsnark/libsnark, plus a ZKCP-style SHA256 hash-locked blockchain payment

rq4.reason_for_choice.sonnet: SNARK offers succinct proofs, zero-knowledge, and rich expressiveness; proving cost is borne by a powerful server. Arithmetic circuits suit ML multiplications.
rq4.reason_for_choice.opus: Low client computation and communication cost, expressiveness, and the zero-knowledge property, which is needed for fair exchange

cq.note.sonnet: The paper discusses ZKCP attacks and malicious client-chosen CRS, and mitigates them through protocol design. It does not study bugs as such.
cq.note.opus: The paper discusses ZKCP attacks such as a client-chosen CRS and argues they do not apply to its setting; it does not study circuit failures.

rq5.limitations.sonnet: Soundness is probabilistic via sampling and relies on the assumption that no shortcut beats the real training algorithm. Delivery correctness of the model is not verified: encryption correctness would need an expensive AES circuit, and the trusted setup is needed.
rq5.limitations.opus: Detection is probabilistic and relies on sampling; the paper assumes the server delivers the real model after verification, and proving encryption of the model in-circuit is too costly. Verification is not economical for tasks with only a few iterations.

rq5.open_problems.sonnet: Malicious aborts and DoS in MLaaS lack a satisfactory deposit-and-refund solution. Better SNARK efficiency and better approximations of non-linear functions are also left open.
rq5.open_problems.opus: Malicious aborts and DoS in MLaaS cannot be handled by the usual deposit/refund schemes. Other open directions are better approximations of non-linear functions and replacing the SNARK with one that needs no trusted setup.
